newsitem.title: MONGOLIA: Mongolia raises budget deficit to 74 bln tugriks.
newsitem.headline: Mongolia raises budget deficit to 74 bln tugriks.

text.p: Mongolia's parliament has approved final changes to the 1997 budget, increasing the deficit to 74 billion tugriks, up from the planned 26.3 billion, officials said on Thursday.

However, the parliament rejected a proposal from the government to cut planned revenues from privatisation and instead insisted the government further boost income from its drive to sell off state firms.
This year's deficit would equal about 10 percent of Gross Domestic Product, parliament members told a news conference.

The Great Hural, or parliament, had approved revenues of 180 billion tugriks, up from a planned 158 billion, and expenditures of 254 billion tugriks, up from 184 billion when the budget was originally approved in December 1996.

The budget had to be reviewed after the government in May scrapped almost all import duties, slashing revenue by more than 10 billion tugriks, and introduced a new mineral law from July reducing mining royalty payments, officials said.
The 22 billion tugrik increase in revenues would be raised through the government's privatisation drive and from increased tax income through more efficient collection, officials said.

Parliament turned down a government proposal to cut revenues from privatisation to 30 billion tugriks from a previous goal of 40 billion tugriks after earning just four billion from privatisation in the first six months, officials said.
Instead the parliament told the government to accelerate privatisation and boost revenues 50 billion tugriks this year.
The government's goal was far too low, Great Hural members said after completing changes to the year budget.
"(The government)... must do the job it is given," D. Ganbold, chairman of the parliament's standing committee on economic policies, told a news conference.
"Privatisation is not proceeding at a satisfactory speed," he said. "It is necessary to speed it up in the second half of the year."

He said privatisation policies were satisfactory, but real action fell short of what the parliament wanted. The government has so far limited privatisation to small properties worth 50-300 million tugriks.
Big firms such as the Gobi Cashmere Factory, numerous mining companies and state shares in petroleum giant NIC and alcohol producer APU had still not be been up for sale, he said.
"It is possible to make multi-billion revenues by privatising these big entities," Ganbold said.
The ruling Democratic Union Coalition has said it would privatise up to 60 percent of total state assets by 2000.
As a result of tax reforms implemented earlier this year, about 70 to 80 percent of all companies in Mongolia would pay lower taxes, officials said.

Budget expenditures had increased due to higher social welfare costs. These included an additional 6.8 billion tugriks for pension funds and 2.8 billion for salary funds as well as 2.5 billion tugriks in subsidies to provincial governments.
"Most increases in expenditure go to the social sector," Ganbold said. "The general direction of government policies in 1997 is toward clear and efficient reforms in the social sector."
Mongolia's budget has been in deficit for the last seven years. Most of this year's deficit would be covered by foreign aid, and part of it by the central bank, he said.
Of total budget expenditures, 78 billion tugriks were covered by foreign aid and loans, the officials said.
Total revenues in 1996 were 159.2 billion tugriks, while total expenditures amounted were 174.2 billion.
